skills.name: Properties of metals explained by metallic bonding

note.text:
Metallic bonding explains the properties of metals:
• Good conductors of electricity: delocalised electrons move through the metal and carry the current.
• Good conductors of heat: free electrons and vibrating ions pass on energy.
• Malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (can be drawn into wires): layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond, because the electron sea moves with them.
• Usually high melting points and high density; shiny (lustrous) when freshly cut; sonorous (ring when struck).
Uses: copper for wires, aluminium for cooking pots and power cables, iron (steel) for building.

sections.heading: Conducting electricity and heat
sections.text:
The delocalised electrons in a metal are free to move. When a battery is connected, they drift through the metal: that is an electric current. So metals conduct electricity even when solid.
They also carry heat energy quickly from hot parts to cold parts, together with the vibrating ions. That is why a metal spoon in hot tea soon feels hot.

sections.heading: Bending without breaking
sections.text:
When a metal is hammered, the layers of ions slide over each other. The sea of electrons moves with them, so the bonding is not broken.
So metals are malleable (can be hammered into sheets, such as roofing sheets) and ductile (can be drawn into wires, such as copper wire).
Compare an ionic crystal: when its layers shift, like charges meet, repel, and it shatters.

sections.heading: Other properties and uses
sections.text:
• Shiny when freshly cut (lustrous) and ringing when struck (sonorous).
• Usually high melting points and high densities (but sodium and potassium are soft, light and low-melting).
Uses follow from properties: copper wires (conducts, ductile), aluminium pots and cables (conducts heat and electricity, light), iron and steel for building (strong).

key_words.meaning: a material that lets electricity or heat pass through easily

mistake.wrong: Metals conduct because their ions move
mistake.right: Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons move
mistake.why: In a solid metal the ions stay in place; only the electrons move freely.

worked_example.problem: Explain why copper is used for electric wires.
steps: Copper has metallic bonding with many delocalised electrons.
These electrons can move through the metal, carrying an electric current.
Copper is also ductile, so it can be drawn into thin wires.
worked_example.answer: It conducts well (free electrons) and is ductile

cards.idea: Free electrons carry electric current through a metal.
Layers of ions slide without breaking the bond: malleable and ductile.
example: Gold can be beaten into very thin sheets.
Aluminium pots conduct heat well and do not rust.

pick.y: Heat passes quickly from the fire to the food.

pick.r: strong and malleable (can be pressed into corrugated sheets)
e: Conductivity is not why it is used for roofs.
Roofing is painted or galvanised, not chosen for shine.

pick.q: Why do metals conduct electricity when solid?
w: Their atoms share pairs of electrons
e: In a solid metal the ions stay in place.
Shared pairs are fixed; they cannot carry current.
pick.y: Moving free electrons carry the current.

pick.q: Why do metals conduct heat well?
pick.r: Free electrons and vibrating ions pass on energy quickly
pick.y: That is why cooking pots are made of metal.

pick.q: Why can metals be bent without breaking?
pick.r: Layers of ions slide over each other and the electron sea keeps them bonded
e: The sea of electrons stops the ions repelling apart.
pick.y: The bonding is not fixed between particular atoms.

questions.prompt: Which property of the metal explains this use? {X.q}

pick.q: A sheet of metal is hammered and bends; a crystal of salt is hammered and shatters. Why the difference?
pick.r: In salt, shifting layers brings like charges together; in a metal the electron sea keeps the ions bonded
pick.y: Ionic lattices are brittle; metallic lattices are malleable.

pick.q: Which property of metals is NOT explained by free electrons?
e: Free electrons reflect light, making metals shiny.
pick.y: Density depends on how heavy the ions are and how closely they pack.

pick.q: Why is aluminium, not copper, used for overhead power cables?
pick.r: It conducts well and is much less dense, so the cables are lighter
pick.y: Light cables need fewer, cheaper pylons.
